# R6 Digest — Absalom’s Rebellion (2 Sam 15–19:8 approx.)
**Source:** Tsumura, *The Second Book of Samuel* (NICOT, 2019)
**Reader:** extraction subagent R6
**Coverage:** slice lines 1–1233 = raw **8449–9681** read in full  
**Body span:** 2 Sam **15:1** through start of **18:33 / MT 19:1** (David’s lament begins).  
**Slice ends mid-sentence** of the “O Absalom” speech; **Joab’s rebuke (19:5–8) is not in this range** (continues in R7).

## Claims

### C-R6-01 | Section division of Absalom’s rebellion (15:1–20:22)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** The long section 15:1–20:22 divides into six parts: Absalom’s conspiracy (15:1-12); David’s escape and people met on the way (15:13–16:14); war council Ahithophel vs Hushai determining David’s fate (16:15–17:23); reception at Mahanaim (17:24-29); battle and death of Absalom (18:1–19:8); return to Jerusalem (19:9-43).
- **Quote:** "The war council where the battle between Ahithophel and Hushai determines David’s fate (16:15–17:23)"
- **Locus:** §B intro / slice L1–14 / raw ~8449–8462
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[absalom]], [[david]]

### C-R6-02 | Root of rebellion: resentment + ambition; divine frame = David’s sin
- **Claim:** The king’s kiss of Absalom (14:33) sounds neutral on reconciliation degree; a root cause of the rebellion is Absalom’s resentment toward his father, though the immediate cause is ambition. From the divine perspective, all calamities David experienced result from his own rebellion against God’s commandments. Losing people’s support and respect is the main reason Absalom can steal the hearts of the men of Israel (15:6).
- **Quote:** "From the divine perspective, all the calamities David experienced are the result of his own rebellion against God’s commandments."
- **Locus:** §B intro / slice L20–22 / raw ~8468–8470
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[nathan]]

### C-R6-03 | Narrative tempo: revolt fast; flight slow
- **Claim:** Story moves first quickly then very slowly: outbreak of premeditated revolt determined and fast (six verses); narration of David’s departure from Jerusalem is sustained tension of thirty-nine verses.
- **Quote:** "The outbreak of the premeditated revolt was determined and fast, narrated in six verses. On the other hand, the narration of David’s departure from Jerusalem is a sustained tension of thirty-nine verses."
- **Locus:** §B intro / slice L24–25 / raw ~8472–8473
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[david]]

### C-R6-04 | Conspiracy as justice-claiming: gate, suit, “appoint me as judge”
- **Claim:** Absalom’s habitual practice (vv. 1-6 SETTING; waw+pf habitual) stations him beside the way to the gate; he flatters litigants that their case is good and straight but they will have no hearing from the king, and wishes someone would appoint him judge in the land so he would give justice. Tsumura notes personal attention from the handsome, accessible royal son is flattering; “you are right” is easy when ignoring the other party.
- **Quote:** "Would that someone appoint me as a judge in the land! Then anyone who had a suit could come to me for judgment and I would give him justice."
- **Locus:** 15:1-6 translation + notes / slice L28–54, L88–90 / raw ~8476–8502, ~8536–8538
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-05 | Absalom’s “justice” claim = “Oh that I were king”
- **Claim:** Absalom appeals to the tradition of the king as judge (Prov. 31:9; Isa. 11:3-5), bound with the Lord as judge—not judgeship of the previous era. He is effectively saying “Oh that I were king!”; chariot and runners (v. 1) and this claim show him acting as heir preparing for kingship. C. H. Gordon compares Absalom’s rebellion in this “royal epic” with crown prince Yassib in Ugaritic Keret; Yassib, like Absalom, claimed motivation by lack of justice.
- **Quote:** "Absalom is here appealing to the tradition of the king as judge… Thus he is saying, “Oh that I were king!”… It is noteworthy that Yassib, like Absalom, claimed to be motivated by a lack of justice."
- **Locus:** 15:4 note / slice L98–98 / raw ~8546–8546
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-06 | “Stole the hearts” = capture affection, not only deceive
- **Claim:** Against McCarter’s preference for “deceive/dupe” (Gen. 31:20), Tsumura—looking at 15:13 “The hearts of the men of Israel have followed Absalom!”—takes “steal the hearts” as “to capture the affection of.” In chs. 15-18 “Israel” usually means Absalom’s side; David’s side is “David’s servants” or “the army.” Nothing suggests Judah did not join: Absalom proclaimed kingship in Hebron; Hushai’s “Dan to Beersheba” (17:11); 19:11-14 implies Judah participated.
- **Quote:** "looking at v. 13… it would seem that here it means “to capture the affection of.”… There is nothing to suggest that Judah did not join."
- **Locus:** 15:6 note / slice L104–106 / raw ~8552–8554
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-07 | “Forty years” (15:7): lectio difficilior; waiting-period formula
- **Claim:** Majority of modern scholars accept “four years” (LXXL, Syr, Vul) or “forty days”; MT “forty years” is lectio difficilior and supported by main LXX tradition. Cannot be fortieth year of David’s reign (he remained king after Absalom’s death). McCarter’s enclitic-m “four years”; Althann’s forced “forty days… spoke insistently.” Tsumura tentatively takes miqqēṣ ʾarbāʿîm šānāh (also Ezek. 29:13) as formulaic for end of a long wandering period: “toward the end of Absalom’s waiting period.”
- **Quote:** "Tentatively, I take the phrase to mean “toward the end of Absalom’s waiting period.”"
- **Locus:** 15:7 note / slice L108–110 / raw ~8556–8558
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R6-08 | Vow in Hebron not “Yahweh-in-Hebron”; sacrifices as coronation
- **Claim:** Against McCarter’s “Yahweh-in-Hebron” local-deity reading: local deities use construct “DN of GN,” not “DN in GN”; “in Hebron” modifies “go and fulfill,” not “made.” Sacrifices announced as vow payment were apparently part of a coronation ceremony asserting kingship (v. 10; 16:16).
- **Quote:** "These sacrifices, while announced as payment of his vow, were apparently actually part of a coronation ceremony, formally asserting his kingship"
- **Locus:** 15:7-8, 12 notes / slice L112–120 / raw ~8560–8568
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-09 | Ahithophel: name possibly “foolishness”; counselor from Giloh
- **Claim:** Element “tophel” of Ahithophel possibly means “foolishness”; otherwise unknown among Hebrew names. McCarter: deliberate distortion satirizing ill-used wisdom (cf. bošet for baʿal). Title counselor (yôʿēṣ); Giloh in Judean hills (Josh. 15:51), south/west of Hebron near Kh. Rabud.
- **Quote:** "The element “tophel” of Ahithophel possibly means “foolishness.”… McCarter suggests that this name is “a deliberate distortion satirizing the man’s ill-used wisdom.”"
- **Locus:** 15:12 note / slice L122–126 / raw ~8570–8574
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]
- **Misc flag:** Ahithophel — substantial; no dedicated target slug assigned

### C-R6-10 | Flight structure: symmetry with return; encounters list
- **Claim:** David flees Jerusalem lest the city be destroyed; Ps 3 said composed on this occasion. On the way he meets: loyal band of foreigners; priests Abiathar and Zadok; friend Hushai; Mephibosheth’s servant Ziba; Benjaminite Shimei. Scholars note symmetry between flight Jerusalem→Jordan (15:13–16:14) and return (19:16[15]–20:3).
- **Quote:** "Scholars have noticed that there is a certain symmetry between the account of David’s flight from Jerusalem to the Jordan (15:13–16:14) and that of his return (19:16[15]–20:3)."
- **Locus:** 15:13–16:14 intro / slice L128–132 / raw ~8576–8580
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]]
- **Misc flag:** Ziba, Shimei — substantial in subsequent claims

### C-R6-11 | David flees to spare the city; ten concubines left
- **Claim:** David orders flight so Absalom not overtake them, bring disaster, and strike the city with the edge of the sword. King and household go out on foot; ten concubines left to keep the house (preparatory for 16:21-22). Stops at the last house before Kidron (bêt hammerḥāq).
- **Quote:** "lest he overtake us quickly and bring disaster upon us and strike the city with the edge of the sword."
- **Locus:** 15:13-17 / slice L133–180 / raw ~8581–8628
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-12 | Cherethites, Pelethites, Gittites; Ittai’s loyalty oath
- **Claim:** Bodyguard Cherethites/Pelethites identified as “Cretans and Philistines.” Gittites (six hundred—standard regiment size) are not David’s old 1 Sam 27 men (came “yesterday”; Ittai a foreigner)—Philistine-style military unit. David invites Ittai to return with the king (Absalom); Ittai swears by the LORD and the king to stay for death or life (Ruth/Naomi parallel). Name-play Ittai / ʾattāh / ʾittānû stresses common fate.
- **Quote:** "surely in the place where my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, there your servant shall be."
- **Locus:** 15:18-22 / slice L162–246 / raw ~8610–8694
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-13 | Ark sent back: not a charm; favor vs no-delight
- **Claim:** Zadok and Levites bring the ark; David commands: take the ark back to the city. If he finds favor in the LORD’s eyes, the LORD will bring him back and show him the ark and its habitation; if the LORD has no delight in him, “let him do to me as it is good in his eyes.” Zadok/Abiathar return the ark to Jerusalem and stay.
- **Quote:** "If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and show it and its habitation to me. But if he should say thus: ‘I have no delight in you,’ here I am, let him do to me as it is good in his eyes."
- **Locus:** 15:24-29 / slice L259–296 / raw ~8707–8744
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R6-14 | Ark decision: not 1 Sam 4 charm; sin-awareness; providence messenger system
- **Claim:** David does not use the ark as a charm (contrast 1 Sam. 4:3). Perhaps because he realizes the rebellion is partly result of his sins (2 Sam. 12:10); he does not know how far the Lord intends to punish him. Mourning/penitence and acceptance of malice (16:10) related. He still considers the rebellion wrong and uses prayer and human opportunities God gives (vv. 28, 31, 34; Neh. 4:9). Though David leaves the city, by providence of God he sets up messenger system: Hushai → Zadok and Abiathar → sons (via maid, 17:17) → David (v. 36).
- **Quote:** "David does not use the ark as a charm, in contrast to the attitude in 1 Sam. 4:3.… Though David leaves the city, by the providence of God he is able to set up a messenger system"
- **Locus:** 15:24-37 notes / slice L298–306 / raw ~8746–8754

### C-R6-15 | “Are you a seer?”; steppes of the wilderness = Jordan Valley
- **Claim:** hărôʾeh ʾattāh most naturally a rhetorical question expecting “No”: “You are no seer!” (vs REB positive; various emendations). David waits in steppes of the wilderness (K. metathesis of Q. beʿarbôt) = Jordan Valley north of Dead Sea; will stop west bank and wait for news (17:16).
- **Quote:** "The most natural translation is a rhetorical question expecting the answer “No.” So, Are you a seer? : i.e., “You are no seer!”"

### C-R6-18 | Ziba’s provisions; gift of Mephibosheth’s estate; possible lie
- **Claim:** Beyond summit, Ziba brings donkeys and food (list similar to Abigail, 1 Sam 25:18). Claims Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping “the house of Israel will be returned to me with my father’s kingdom.” David gives all that belongs to Mephibosheth to Ziba—shows human kings could transfer grants. Mephibosheth later (19:24-27) claims Ziba lied. Divided feelings / Benjaminite residual hostility may have made David sensitive; Ziba used this. Scenario barely practical; even Shimei did not suggest restoring Saul’s house that way.

### C-R6-19 | Shimei’s curse: man of blood; blood of house of Saul
- **Claim:** At Bahurim, Shimei son of Gera (clan of house of Saul) curses continually and stones David: “man of blood,” “worthless man”; the LORD has returned blood of house of Saul and given kingdom to Absalom. Shimei probably blames David for Abner and Ish-bosheth deaths, possibly Saul’s sons/grandsons (ch. 21) or even Saul—not necessarily actual complicity. Writer of Samuel goes to great lengths to absolve David; residual ill-feeling toward David re house of Saul remained when Samuel was written; curse contexts become hyperbolic.

### C-R6-20 | David accepts Shimei’s curse as from the LORD; hope of good return
- **Claim:** Abishai offers to behead the “dead dog”; David: “What is it to me and to you, O sons of Zeruiah… For the LORD said to him ‘Curse David!’” Even his own son seeks his life; how much more this Benjaminite. Let him curse, for the LORD has told him. Perhaps the LORD will look at his eyes (Q. beʿênî; K. beʿăwōnî “my guilt”—Tiqqun sopherim) and return good for the cursing. Not a Deuteronomistic anticipation of 1 K. 2 Shimei execution (contra Veijola); similar to David’s reply to Abishai in 1 Sam. 26:8-11. Taking Abishai’s advice would be disastrous for David.
- **Quote:** "For the LORD said to him ‘Curse David!’ Who can say, ‘Why have you done this?’… Perhaps the LORD will look at my eyes and the LORD will return good to me in return for his cursing this day."

### C-R6-22 | Ahithophel’s “good counsel” would have destroyed weary David
- **Claim:** Ahithophel’s sound proposal: attack and kill David immediately; country would then embrace Absalom. If this “good counsel” (v. 14) had been followed, David’s large weary/exhausted group (16:14) would likely have been destroyed. Absalom hears Hushai also—trusts him enough to hear, not enough to include in war-council deliberations. Hushai’s flattering, time-consuming, simile-filled speech lets David regroup; Hushai sends warning to cross Jordan even before hearing the council result.
- **Quote:** "If this “good counsel” (v. 14) had been followed, it is likely that David, whose large group was indeed weary and exhausted (16:14), would have been destroyed."

- **Claim (Tsumura citing Bergen):** Ahithophel’s counsel incorporates three hallmarks of classic military strategy: overwhelming force, surprise, narrowly focused objective—twelve thousand, pursue tonight, attack while weary/exhausted, terrify so people flee, strike only the king, bring people back to peace. ### C-R6-26 | Hushai’s speech: similes, slow action, flattery of Absalom as leader
- **Claim:** Longest speech in Absalom-rebellion story; dramatic turning point; critical for united monarchy history. Ahithophel: straightforward terse “unembellished string of verbs.” Hushai nearly triple length, suggesting slowing of action. Metaphors: bear robbed of cubs; David won’t spend night with people; hides in pits; first fall → panic “slaughter among people who follow Absalom”; even lion-hearted will faint. ### C-R6-34 | Absalom caught by head in oak; hair-reading popular but not required
- **Claim:** Absalom on mule under thick branches of great oak; head caught fast; set between heaven and earth; mule goes on. “Hanging” in v. 10—too much to force Deut. 21:23 curse (contra Bergen). From Josephus on, popular that hair he prided himself on (14:26) tangled; Ackerman’s Gen 22 ram association “farfetched.” Tsumura rejects Brueggemann’s claim that text is “very difficult”/obscure for dark theology—Hebrew has no textual problem; “head” can be synecdoche for hair. Such “theological” comment only by reading own ideas into text without solid basis.
- **Quote:** "the Hebrew text here has no textual problem and there is no reason why Brueggemann should say it is “a very difficult text.”… If such is a “theological” comment, one can do so only by reading one’s own ideas into the ancient text without a solid basis."

### C-R6-35 | Joab kills Absalom against David’s order (and the man’s refusal)
- **Claim:** Informant refuses Joab’s rebuke for not killing Absalom—would not for a thousand shekels; in their hearing the king commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai to protect Absalom; nothing hidden from king though Joab may stand aloof.
